newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Norilsk sale up in the air with only hours to go.
newsitem.headline: Norilsk sale up in the air with only hours to go.

text.p: The fate of the sale of a controlling stake in Russia's Norilsk Nickel, one of the world's biggest mining companies, hung in the balance on the very day the winner of the tender was scheduled to have been announced.

Norilsk officials on Tuesday could shed little light on the murky events surrounding the next controversial round of state privatisation, which has rocked Russia's commercial and political edifice to the core.
"Until very recently there was never any reason to doubt that the tender would go ahead as planned," said Sergei Vetchinin, Norilsk's Moscow-based spokesman.

"But you have heard the reports that (Russian Prime Minister Viktor) Chernomyrdin has ordered the property fund to stop the auction, so I can't say with complete certainty whether there will be a tender or not."
Chernomyrdin instructed the Federal Property Committee on Thursday to suspend the sale of a 38 percent share in Norilsk less than 24 hours before the winner was to have been named.

But a senior source at commercial bank Uneximbank, which controls the 38 percent stake, repeated Monday's statement that the winner of the tender would be announced, but a little later than originally planned -- at around 5 p.m. local time (1300 GMT).

The controversy about the auction casts doubt over RAO Norilsky Nikel's plans to double its share capital by issuing 126 million ordinary shares, and convert its existing preferred shares to voting ordinary stock.
News of the possible suspension of the auction caused the preferred shares, worth less than ordinaries, to fall sharply on Monday after rising on news of the conversion last week.

Uneximbank got control of the 38 percent, which represents 51 percent of voting shares, in 1995 under the shares-for-loans scheme. It put the block up for sale in line with the conditions of the original deal with the state, and was widely tipped to emerge victorious in the tender.
That was until about two weeks ago, when an unprecedented wave of media protest and mud-slinging followed the sale of a 25 percent stake in telecoms holding company Svyazinvest.

Uneximbank led the winning consortium, but Russian media, controlled by powerful tycoons who participants in the auction have said belong to the losing consortium, attacked the sale and demanded the conditions be reviewed.
The spotlight quickly turned to Norilsk, a much more obvious target for accusations of closed deals and unfair competition.
Uneximbank has said all along that foreign companies could not bid for the stake, drastically reducing the number of potential competitors.
Bank MFK (ICFI in English), which is organising the tender, is also the investment arm of Uneximbank -- a link which has raised a few eyebrows in the domestic and foreign press.
Some analysts view Chernomyrdin's order as brinkmanship, which he may use to squeeze a few more dollars out of Uneximbank president Vladimir Potanin in the Norilsk sale.

But he has considerable leverage, considering that the state officially owns the Norilsk stake and that the possibility of an investigation into the conditions of the Svyazinvest tender still looms over Potanin.
Whatever the outcome of the Norilsk sale, it is unlikely to be the last chapter in the ownership saga.
"Regardless of the results that are announced, it is clear that we are a long way from any clarity on the company's long- term ownership," Pioneer Securities said in a market commentary.
Norilsk is the world's largest supplier of palladium, is vying to become the biggest nickel producer this year, and is a major producer of platinum, copper and cobalt.
Its production arm is profitable, but huge costs associated with supporting the remote Arctic city of Norilsk have sapped its resources, turning it into a loss-making monolith.

Uneximbank management has succeeded in hiving off some social costs on to local authorities, reducing wage arrears at the group's flagship metals combine and boosting production significantly during the last year or so.
But even this may not be enough to quell the storm surrounding the tender.
Norilsk is part of a round of state property sell-offs in Russia, which in 1997 could raise between $4-5 billion for state coffers.
